amaro-del-capo: Amaro del Capo comes from the Caffo family: in 1915 Giuseppe Caffo, a master distiller, founded a distillery at Santa Venerina, on the slopes of Etna, working at first with grape marc and wine by-products. His sons moved the business to Limbadi, in the Calabrian province of Vibo Valentia, and in 1965 the house created Vecchio Amaro del Capo from twenty-nine Calabrian herbs, flowers, fruits and roots, which became its flagship. There is also a version made with Calabrian chilli.
zucca-rabarbaro: Rabarbaro Zucca takes its name from Ettore Zucca, who created it in Milan in 1845 by steeping rhubarb root with bitter orange peel, cardamom and other aromatics, so the name has nothing to do with zucca, the pumpkin. It became one of the classic aperitivi of Milan. From the mid-1990s until 2012 its name replaced Camparino on the sign of the historic café at the entrance to the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II, and the brand now belongs to ILLVA Saronno.
china-martini: China Martini comes from Martini & Rossi, the Turin vermouth house, and belongs to the china family of Italian bitters, named not for the country but for cinchona bark, china calissaia in Italian, the source of quinine, and pronounced kee-na. It is made from the bark with a mixture of aromatic herbs and essences. Its cinchona recalls how many nineteenth-century bitters were first sold as tonics rather than as drinks.
cocchi-americano: Giulio Cocchi, a Florentine pastry maker, settled in Asti in 1891 and began making aromatised wines, and by the turn of the century his Barolo Chinato and Aperitivo Americano were exported to London, New York, Africa and South America. The name is usually traced to amaro, bitter, rather than to America. After Lillet reformulated Kina Lillet in 1986 and softened its quinine, bartenders adopted Cocchi Americano as the nearest match for a period Vesper.
bonal: Bonal was created in 1865 by Hippolyte Bonal, who is said to have been raised and trained at the Grande Chartreuse monastery and to have served as the abbey's doctor before settling as a pharmacist in nearby Saint-Laurent-du-Pont. Drawing on the gentian, cinchona and herbs of the Chartreuse mountains, he made a fortified aperitif and sold it with the promise ouvre l'appétit, the opener of the appetite.
byrrh: Byrrh was created in 1866 in Thuir, in Roussillon, by the brothers Pallade and Simon Violet, travelling drapers turned wine merchants, who blended local wine and mistelle with cinchona and sold it as a tonic wine, at first through pharmacies. By tradition the name comes from the letters B, Y, R, R and H on a colour chart for the fabrics they sold, and it was registered as a trademark in 1873. Since 1950 the Thuir cellars have held an oak vat of about a million litres, often called the largest in the world.
dubonnet: By the usual account, in 1846 the French government sought a way to make quinine palatable to Foreign Legionnaires in North Africa, where malaria was rife, and Joseph Dubonnet, a Paris wine merchant and chemist, answered with a sweet fortified wine infused with cinchona bark, herbs and spices. The aperitif outgrew its medicinal purpose and became a fixture of French cafés. In Britain it found royal admirers: Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother was famously fond of Dubonnet with gin, a taste Elizabeth II was widely reported to share.
amer-picon: Gaétan Picon, a distiller trained in Provence who served with the French army in Algeria, created his bitter orange aperitif there in 1837, by the usual account, first calling it Amer Africain. He went on to open distilleries at Philippeville, Constantine, Bône and Algiers, and a bronze medal at the London exhibition of 1862 helped spread the name. In 1872 he returned to France and founded the Marseille factory, and Picon became a staple of French bars, best known stirred into beer as a Picon bière.
salers: Salers dates from 1885, when Alfred Labounoux began making a gentian liqueur at Montaignac-Saint-Hippolyte, in Corrèze, and named it after Salers, the old town of the Cantal uplands where wild gentian grows. It is often described as the oldest gentian aperitif still made in France. In 2006 the brand joined the Védrenne family group and moved to Turenne, also in Corrèze, where it is now made under the Distillerie des Terres Rouges name.
aveze: Avèze traces back to 1929, when Émile Refouvelet, who kept a delicatessen at Riom-ès-Montagnes, in the Cantal, began selling a gentian aperitif of his own making in his shop. It was sold for years under the name Auvergne before taking the Avèze name in the 1960s. It is made from the roots of yellow gentian, which grows wild in the volcanic uplands of the Massif Central around the town.
peychauds-bitters: Antoine Amédée Peychaud, a Creole apothecary from Saint-Domingue, now Haiti, made his aromatic bitters in New Orleans; popular accounts date them to the 1830s, while other sources place them between 1849 and 1857. They became the defining ingredient of the city's Sazerac, and the Sazerac Company makes them today. A popular story says Peychaud served brandy and bitters in an egg cup called a coquetier and that the word cocktail grew from it, but the word was in print before his drinks were, so the tale is treated as legend.
orange-bitters: Orange bitters, a tincture built on dried bitter orange peel with spices such as cardamom and caraway, were a standard bottle in nineteenth-century bars on both sides of the Atlantic and appear throughout early Martini recipes. After Prohibition they almost disappeared, kept alive in America largely by Fee Brothers of Rochester. Their comeback came when the writer and bartender Gary Regan developed Regans' Orange Bitters No. 6 with the Sazerac Company, just as the classic cocktail revival took hold.
malort: Malört is Swedish for wormwood, and Chicago's version follows the Swedish habit of wormwood-flavoured brännvin. Carl Jeppson, a Swedish immigrant, made it in Chicago and during Prohibition sold it door to door as a medicine, and it was officially introduced in the city in 1933, after repeal. The lawyer George Brode later acquired the formula, and its famously harsh taste turned Jeppson's Malört into a Chicago institution and something close to a civic drink.
fernet: Fernet is the bitterest family of Italian amari, and its archetype, Fernet-Branca, was created in Milan in 1845 by Bernardino Branca, who sold it as a stomach tonic. Where the word fernet comes from is uncertain, and the stories of a doctor named Fernet are not documented. Italian emigrants carried the style to Argentina, where fernet with cola became a national institution, and in San Francisco it became a bartenders' calling card.
kuemmerling: Hugo Kümmerling began developing a herbal liqueur in 1921 in Deesbach, in the Thuringian Forest, and settled on its secret formula in 1938. After the war the business left Thuringia, moving to Coburg in Bavaria in 1949 and then to Bodenheim, near Mainz, in 1963, and in the 1950s his son-in-law Johannes Persch built up its industrial production and marketing. The tiny single-measure bottle became its trademark.
killepitsch: Killepitsch comes from the Busch family of Düsseldorf. Family tradition says its name was born in an air-raid shelter during the Second World War, in a conversation between Willi Busch and his friend Hans Müller-Schlösser, author of the comedy Schneider Wibbel, about what they would do if they came out alive. It was first served to the public in 1955, through the small window of the family's Et Kabüffke tasting room in the old town, and its recipe of 98 herb, berry and fruit essences is still a family secret.
blutwurz: Blutwurz, blood root, is named for tormentil, Potentilla erecta, whose cut rhizome turns red and colours the liqueur, a plant with a long history in central European folk medicine. The roots are chopped and macerated with other herbs and spices, giving a strong, dry and astringent spirit that the Bavarian Forest has made its own. A prominent name is Penninger of Hauzenberg, a family distillery founded early in the twentieth century.
genziana: Genziana is the gentian-root liqueur of the Abruzzo, made by steeping the roots in wine or spirit to farmhouse recipes across the Apennines, a tradition with no single recorded origin.
fernet-vallet: Henri Vallet, a French entrepreneur who came to Mexico in the time of Emperor Maximilian, founded his liqueur company in Mexico City in 1882, though some accounts give a later date, bringing with him the recipes and methods of French bitters. He stayed on after the empire fell, and his Fernet-Vallet and Amargo Vallet became fixtures of Mexican bar culture. The company says the bitters are still made to his original formulas, giving Mexico a fernet tradition of its own.
amaro-sibilla: Amaro Sibilla comes from the Varnelli family of the Sibillini mountains, whose liqueur business dates from 1868, when Girolamo Varnelli, a herbalist at Cupi di Visso, is said to have devised a bitter remedy for the fevers that struck shepherds on their seasonal migrations. The house describes it as still made the old way, with gentian, cinchona and other plants decocted over a wood fire and sweetened with honey. The Varnelli distillery now works at Muccia, in the province of Macerata.
select-aperitivo: Select was created in Venice in 1920 by the brothers Mario and Vittorio Pilla, whose liqueur firm, Fratelli Pilla & C., set out to take part in the city's revival after the First World War. In 1954 the brand passed to Distilleria Jean Buton, later absorbed into Gruppo Montenegro, which still makes it to the original recipe. Select became a fixture of the city's bars and the traditional bitter of the Venetian spritz.
cappelletti-aperitivo: The Cappelletti business began in Trento in 1909, founded by Giuseppe Cappelletti, and it is still owned by his family, now producing at Aldeno, south of the city, among vineyards and orchards. Its red aperitivo is built on white wine rather than neutral spirit, which keeps it lower in strength than its Milanese rivals. It is still coloured with carmine from cochineal, a practice Campari abandoned in 2006.
petrus-boonekamp: Petrus Boonekamp dates itself to 1777 and to a Dutch maker of that name, while German sources place the first such bitter around 1780 at Leidschendam, made by an apothecary remembered as Boonekamp or Kamp. The name became a byword for a style of magenbitter, above all in Germany, where an 1894 trademark law left it free for any distiller to use. The Petrus Boonekamp brand changed hands several times and now belongs to Italy's Gruppo Caffo 1915.
amaro-ciociaro: Amaro Ciociaro is made by Paolucci Liquori of Sora, in the province of Frosinone, and the company presents it as a family recipe dating back to 1873. Its name refers to Ciociaria, the traditional name for that hill country of southern Lazio. The recipe is secret but built on bitter orange, which is why American bartenders took it up as a stand-in for Amer Picon after the French original was reformulated and became hard to find abroad.
ferro-china: Ferro China is the Italian family of amari made with cinchona bark and an iron salt, and its founding brand, Ferro-China Bisleri, was patented in 1881 by the Milanese chemist Felice Bisleri. It was sold in its day as a tonic, and the iron still gives it a faint metallic edge. The category faded in the later twentieth century, leaving a handful of makers such as the Roman house Baliva to carry it on.
amaro-nardini: Bortolo Nardini settled in Bassano del Grappa in 1779 and opened a grapperia at the eastern end of the Ponte Vecchio, distilling grappa from pomace in copper stills. Still run by his descendants, the house is often described as Italy's oldest distillery, and the grapperia on the bridge still serves. Its amaro, built on a grappa base rather than neutral spirit, is a later addition to a house built on grappa.
rabarbaro: Rabarbaro is the family of Italian amari built on dried Chinese rhubarb root, Rheum palmatum, a botanical long traded into Europe, with Milan's Zucca the most famous name in the style.
creme-de-cacao: Crème de cacao is a sweet French-style liqueur of cacao beans and vanilla, made clear or dark, its name referring to its high sugar content rather than to any cream.
creme-de-banane: Crème de banane is a banana liqueur in the French crème tradition and a long-standing tiki and dessert-drink ingredient, with no single recorded inventor.
creme-de-mure: Crème de mûre is a French-style blackberry liqueur, the one Dick Bradsell drizzled over crushed ice to finish his Bramble in London.
creme-de-noyaux: Crème de noyaux is a French-style liqueur that takes its almond flavour from apricot and cherry kernels rather than almonds, and it is what turns a Pink Squirrel pink.
melon-liqueur: The melon liqueur most drinkers know began in Japan in 1964, when Suntory released it as Hermes Melon Liqueur. Renamed Midori, the Japanese word for green, it was launched in the United States in 1978 with a party at New York's Studio 54, and it was made only in Japan until 1987. Its vivid green colour made it a fixture of the cocktails of the following decade.
black-raspberry-liqueur: The most familiar black raspberry liqueur, Chambord, was developed in 1982 by Norton Cooper at his family's Philadelphia cordial firm, Charles Jacquin et Cie, and is made in the Loire Valley from raspberries, vanilla, citrus peel, honey and cognac. Its makers tie it to a legend that Louis XIV was served a wild-raspberry liqueur on a visit to the Château de Chambord in the late seventeenth century. Brown-Forman has owned the brand since 2006, and Cooper's son Robert went on to create St-Germain.
coconut-rum-liqueur: The coconut rum most bars know, Malibu, was created in 1978 by Tom Jago of International Distillers and Vintners and was first made in Curaçao, as a way to make piña coladas simpler for bartenders. When it took off, production moved to Barbados, where the rum comes from the West Indies Rum Distillery. Pernod Ricard has owned the brand since 2005.
anisette: Marie Brizard, the daughter of a Bordeaux distiller, founded her liqueur house in the city in 1755 with Jean-Baptiste Roger, the husband of one of her nieces, and her anisette made Bordeaux's name in the style. Legend says she nursed a sick West Indian sailor who repaid her with the recipe, a story that cannot be verified. Her anisette found favour at the court of Louis XV, and the founders' descendants were still among the company's leaders ten generations later.
chinchon: Vines and anise have long been grown around Chinchón, south-east of Madrid, and in 1911 local growers founded the Sociedad Cooperativa Alcoholera de Chinchón to distil and bottle the town's anise on an industrial scale. The name later gained legal protection as a geographical indication for anise spirit. It is made in dry, sweet and extra-strong versions, and the extra-strong seco especial is among the strongest anise spirits sold.
herbsaint: Herbsaint was created in New Orleans in 1934 by J. Marion Legendre and Reginald Parker, who had learned about absinthe in France during the First World War. It was first sold as Legendre Absinthe, although it contained no grand wormwood, and when federal regulators objected to the word it became Legendre Herbsaint, from herbe sainte, the Creole French name for wormwood. The Sazerac Company bought the Legendre firm in 1949, and Herbsaint is the traditional rinse for a New Orleans Sazerac.
kummel: The earliest known kümmel recipe, attributed to a knight of the Livonian Order, dates from 1503, and a legend credits Lucas Bols with distilling it in the Netherlands in 1575, before he was born. The style flourished in the Baltic: by 1823 Wilhelm von Blanckenhagen was making it on his estate at Allasch, near Riga, and by the mid-nineteenth century Ludwig Mentzendorff was importing kümmel to Britain. In Scottish golf clubhouses it earned the nickname putting mixture, for its supposed effect on the nerves.
cinnamon-schnapps: Cinnamon schnapps is a sweet, hot cinnamon-flavoured spirit popularised by Swiss and American brands, some suspending gold flakes in the bottle in the manner of the old Danzig Goldwasser.
parfait-amour: Parfait amour, French for perfect love, is a violet-coloured liqueur of citrus, flowers, vanilla and almond made in France and the Netherlands, with no recorded inventor.
pistachio-liqueur: Pistachio liqueur is a relatively modern Sicilian speciality made from the pistachios of Bronte, on the slopes of Etna, in both cream and clear styles.
nocello: Nocello is made by Toschi, the company Giancarlo and Lanfranco Toschi founded in Vignola, near Modena, in 1945 to preserve the town's famous cherries in spirit. The firm, now based at Savignano sul Panaro, added a traditional nocino in the 1960s and Nocello in the 1980s. Where nocino is made from green walnuts picked in early summer, Nocello is a lighter, sweeter liqueur of walnut and hazelnut.
solerno: The most prominent Sicilian blood orange liqueur, Solerno, was launched by William Grant & Sons in the late 2000s and created by Lesley Gracie, the distiller behind Hendrick's Gin. It is made from hand-picked Sanguinello blood oranges grown on the slopes of Etna, together with Sicilian lemons. The fruit's colour comes from anthocyanins that develop when nights turn cold, which is why the volcano's altitude matters to the crop.
bergamot-liqueur: Bergamot liqueur is a southern Italian speciality made from the Calabrian bergamot, the perfumed citrus grown mostly along a narrow coastal strip of Calabria and best known for flavouring Earl Grey tea.
ratafia-catalana: Ratafia catalana is a traditional Catalan liqueur of green walnuts and many herbs, macerated in the sun through the summer to family recipes, and its origins are not documented.
palo-de-mallorca: Palo de Mallorca grew out of the Balearic apothecary tradition: cinchona bark reached Spain from Peru in the seventeenth century, when the islands' marshy coasts still bred malaria, and bitter infusions of it, often with gentian, were taken against fever. Sweetened with sugar and caramel to make them palatable and fortified with alcohol, they became a dark bitter liqueur, made commercially since the nineteenth century. Palo de Mallorca is now a protected geographical designation.
guavaberry: Guavaberry liqueur is Sint Maarten's traditional Christmas drink, made in island homes for generations from rum, cane sugar and wild guavaberries, a fruit unrelated to the guava.
sorrel-liqueur: Sorrel liqueur bottles a Caribbean Christmas tradition, hibiscus calyces steeped with rum, ginger and clove, and it has no single recorded origin.
ponche-kuba: By its maker's account, Ponche Kuba dates from 1942, when the Curaçao merchant Jaime Sprock travelled to Cuba and tasted the homemade cream liqueurs islanders called ponche. He combined what he learned into one recipe of rum, milk, egg and spice, named it Ponche Kuba and made it through his firm, J.A.J. Sprock, on Curaçao. It became a Christmas staple across the Dutch Caribbean islands and Venezuela, where it shares the season with the local ponche crema.
licor-de-cafe: Costa Rican coffee liqueur is built on cane spirit and the country's high-grown coffee, notably from Tarrazú, a drier and more roast-led take on the style.
yuzushu: Yuzushu is a Japanese liqueur of yuzu steeped in shochu or sake, part of the country's broad tradition of fruit liqueurs, with no single recorded origin.
maesilju: Maesil-ju is the Korean liqueur of unripe maesil plums steeped in soju with sugar, made both at home and commercially from the same fruit as Japanese umeshu.
lychee-liqueur: Lychee liqueur is a perfumed infusion of lychee in neutral spirit, made in France and China, and it is the base of the Lychee Martini.
ginger-liqueur: Ginger liqueur is fresh ginger macerated into a spirit base, often cognac or eau-de-vie in the French versions, a style with no single recorded origin.
apricot-brandy-liqueur: Apricot brandy in old cocktail books usually means a sweet apricot liqueur made across Europe rather than a true apricot eau-de-vie, a naming muddle with no single origin.
sea-buckthorn-liqueur: Sea buckthorn liqueur is made in the Nordic and Baltic countries from the sharp orange berries of a shrub that grows on northern coastal dunes, with no single recorded origin.
lingonberry-liqueur: Lingonberry liqueur steeps the tart wild berries of Swedish and Finnish forests in grain spirit, a Nordic speciality with no single recorded origin.
rum-cream: Jamaica's rum cream is closely tied to Sangster's Original Jamaica Rum Cream, created by Dr Ian Sangster, who had come to the island to lecture at the University of the West Indies and later left teaching to make liqueurs. He blended Jamaican rum with dairy cream and a mix of Jamaican fruits and spices, giving the island a cream liqueur of its own just as cream liqueurs were taking off abroad.
dulce-de-leche-liqueur: Dulce de leche liqueur is a modern Argentine cream liqueur built on the caramelised milk spread that Argentina and Uruguay both claim as their own.
crema-de-orujo: Crema de orujo is a Galician cream liqueur of pomace brandy, cream, coffee and sugar, a modern after-dinner companion to the region's clear and herbal orujo.
grande-champagne-cognac: Cognac's brandy trade grew from the seventeenth century, but its crus took shape in 1860, when the geologist Henri Coquand, working with a taster, classified the region's soils by the quality of brandy they gave. The Cognac area was delimited by decree in 1909 and the six crus confirmed in 1938, with Grande Champagne, on thick Cretaceous chalk around Segonzac, as the first cru. Its name has nothing to do with sparkling wine: champagne means open country, a term shared with the wine region.
petite-champagne-cognac: Petite Champagne rings Grande Champagne on slightly less chalky soil, and like its neighbour it owes its standing to the soil survey Henri Coquand made in 1860. The crus were fixed by decree in 1938, and Cognac's rules define Fine Champagne as a blend of Grande and Petite Champagne eaux-de-vie with at least half from Grande Champagne. Petite Champagne is the other half of a style on which houses such as Rémy Martin have built their range.
borderies-cognac: The Borderies, north of the town of Cognac, is the smallest of the six crus, with roughly 4,000 hectares of vines on clay and flint left by decomposed limestone rather than on chalk. Henri Coquand's soil classification of 1860 set it apart, and the decree of 1938 confirmed it as a cru. Its eaux-de-vie are round and fine, known for a scent of violets, which makes them prized by blenders and keeps single-cru Borderies bottlings rare.
fins-bois-cognac: Fins Bois is the largest of the Cognac crus, a broad ring of vineyards around the Champagnes and the Borderies on soils of clay, limestone and stony ground. Its place in the hierarchy goes back to Henri Coquand's soil classification of 1860, confirmed by the decree of 1938 that grouped the outer crus as the Bois. Quicker to mature, with notes of pressed grape and fruit, it forms the backbone of many VS and VSOP blends.
cognac-hors-dage: Hors d'âge, beyond age, is the term Cognac houses use for their oldest blends, and the industry body, the BNIC, treats it as equivalent to XO. Under the current rules the youngest eau-de-vie in such a blend must have spent at least ten years in oak, a minimum raised from six when the XO rules changed. In practice houses reserve the term for blends far older than that, where the nutty, oxidative note called rancio becomes the point.
bas-armagnac: Armagnac's makers point to 1310, when the prelate Vital du Four listed forty virtues of an aqua ardens, as the oldest written record of any French brandy. The Fallières decree of 1909 drew the region's three districts, and Bas-Armagnac, on sandy, acidic soils in the west, gives the majority of production. The appellation followed in 1936, and the district's eaux-de-vie, traditionally made in the single-column alambic armagnacais, are highly prized.
tenareze: Ténarèze is the central district of Armagnac, on clay and limestone between Bas-Armagnac and Haut-Armagnac, one of the three zones drawn by the Fallières decree of 1909 and confirmed when Armagnac became an appellation in 1936. It gives around two-fifths of all Armagnac, firmer and more structured spirits that need longer in wood. Folle Blanche, the delicate grape that phylloxera nearly wiped out in the late nineteenth century, is among its traditional varieties.
blanche-armagnac: For generations Armagnac producers kept back some of their freshly distilled spirit for their own use, but it could not be sold as Armagnac until 2005, when growers won a separate appellation, Blanche Armagnac. Instead of ageing in oak, it rests in inert containers that keep its aromas and clarity, giving a clear, floral and fruity spirit that shows the grapes directly.
calvados-pays-dauge: Calvados Pays d'Auge, the most demanding of the three Calvados appellations, was given its protected name in 1942. It covers the Pays d'Auge, at the eastern end of the Calvados department and into neighbouring districts, and it is the only Calvados that must be double-distilled in pot stills. Cider distilling in Normandy is far older: the earliest known record comes from the diary of the squire Gilles de Gouberville in 1553, and a guild of cider distillers followed in 1606.
calvados-domfrontais: Calvados Domfrontais is the youngest of the three Calvados appellations, created in 1997 for the pear-growing country around Domfront in southern Normandy. Its rules require at least 30% perry pears in the base, many producers use far more, and the spirit is distilled in column stills. The area's tall perry pear trees, some said to be two centuries old, give the brandy a lighter, more floral character than the apple-led appellations.
pommeau-de-normandie: Pommeau, fresh cider-apple must stopped with Calvados before it can ferment, was made by Norman cider producers for centuries as a way to keep the taste of the juice for months. For a long time it could not be sold commercially, until a dispensation late in the twentieth century let it onto the market as a cider-based aperitif, and it later received its own appellation as Pommeau de Normandie. It is aged in oak before release.
macvin-du-jura: Macvin is an old Jura speciality, documented since at least the fourteenth century under names such as maquevin and marc-vin, and local tradition credits the recipe to the abbesses of Château-Chalon. It began as a cooked, spiced wine preparation; the modern method, blending unfermented grape must with the region's own marc, came later. Macvin du Jura became an appellation late in the twentieth century and shares the nutty, oxidative character of the Jura's wines.
pisco-puro: Pisco puro, made from a single grape variety, is one of the categories set out in Peru's technical standard for pisco. Peruvian rules forbid adding water after distillation, so a pisco puro goes into the bottle at the strength it came off the still, with no wood ageing. Peru protects pisco as its own denomination of origin, a claim to the name that Chile disputes, since it also makes a spirit called pisco.
pisco-acholado: Acholado, Peruvian Spanish for mixed, is pisco made from two or more grape varieties, either fermented together or blended after distillation. It is one of the categories set out in Peru's technical standard for pisco, and a blend lets the distiller balance aromatic and non-aromatic grapes, which makes acholado a common choice for a Pisco Sour.
pisco-mosto-verde: Mosto verde, green must, is pisco distilled before fermentation has finished, so some of the grape's natural sugar is still in the must when it reaches the still. The yeast is not killed; the distiller simply runs the wine early, which takes considerably more grapes per bottle and gives a silkier spirit. It is one of the categories recognised in Peru's technical standard for pisco.
pisco-quebranta: Quebranta is Peru's signature non-aromatic pisco grape, a variety that arose in the country from vines brought by the Spanish. DNA analysis suggests it is a natural cross of Listán Prieto, the Mission grape, and Negramoll. Earthy and restrained rather than floral, it is the traditional base of a Pisco Sour and the usual grape of a pisco puro, and the Ica region on the southern coast is its heartland.
pisco-italia: Pisco Italia is made from the Italia grape, a table variety bred in Italy early in the twentieth century by Alberto Pirovano, who crossed Bicane with Muscat Hamburg. The grape travelled to Peru, where it became one of the four varieties the country classes as aromatic, alongside Torontel, Moscatel and Albilla. Its Muscat parentage shows in the glass, making this the most overtly perfumed of the Peruvian piscos.
brandy-de-penedes: Catalans trace their distilling to the thirteenth-century physician Arnau de Vilanova, who wrote about aqua vitae, but aged Penedès brandy as a product dates from 1928, when Juan Torres Casals, of the Torres wine family of Vilafranca del Penedès, distilled the region's white wines and aged them in oak. Torres became the name most associated with it. Brandy del Penedès now holds a protected geographical indication of its own, separate from Brandy de Jerez.
aguardente-lourinha: The Lourinhã area, on the coast north of Lisbon, was demarcated for brandy in 1992, creating Portugal's only appellation dedicated to wine brandy. With Cognac and Armagnac, it is often described as one of just three demarcated wine-brandy regions in Europe. Its aguardente is distilled from light, acidic base wines and aged in oak, and its main producers are Quinta do Rol and the Adega Cooperativa da Lourinhã.
kanyak: Kanyak, simply a Turkish spelling of cognac, is the name for Turkey's oak-aged grape brandy, long produced by the former state monopoly Tekel.
divin: In Moldova, brandy made by the classic French method and aged in oak is called divin, because cognac is a protected French name; in Romanian the word also means divine. One of the leading producers, the KVINT distillery in Tiraspol, made only vodka from its founding in the late nineteenth century until 1938, when it began producing brandy. Moldova has grown wine grapes for millennia, and divin remains one of its signature exports.
zwetschgenwasser: Zwetschgenwasser is the clear plum brandy of southern Germany and Alsace, distilled from the small oval Zwetschge plum in a farmhouse tradition with no single recorded origin.
mirabelle: The small golden mirabelle plum spread across Lorraine at the end of the nineteenth century, when orchards replaced vineyards devastated by phylloxera, and distilling the crop became a regional tradition. Mirabelle de Lorraine eau-de-vie is now a protected appellation whose zone covers parts of the four Lorraine departments, Meurthe-et-Moselle, Meuse, Moselle and Vosges, across more than a thousand communes. The fruit's season is short, and the region's distillers work to it.
quetsch: Quetsch is the clear Alsatian brandy of the purple quetsche plum, the same fruit as the German Zwetschge, made in a farm-distilling tradition with no single recorded origin.
himbeergeist: Himbeergeist is the German and Alsatian raspberry spirit made by macerating the fruit in alcohol and redistilling it, the Geist method used for fruit too low in sugar to ferment.
vieille-prune: Vieille prune, plum brandy aged in oak until it turns amber, is closely tied to Souillac, in the Lot, where Louis Roque founded his distillery in 1905 on the site of an old convent. He came from a family of distillers, and he became the local specialist in plum brandy, ageing it slowly in casks. After the First World War he refined the recipe, and La Vieille Prune, created in 1920, became the house signature, still made by the family's fifth generation.
eau-de-vie-de-coing: Quince eau-de-vie is a rare and costly fruit brandy of Alsace and central Europe, distilled from a hard, astringent fruit that yields little juice, with no single recorded origin.
holunder-geist: Holunderbeergeist is an Austrian and German elderberry spirit made by maceration and redistillation, because the berries carry too little sugar to ferment usefully.
sorb-eau-de-vie: Eau-de-vie de sorbier is a rare Alpine and central European spirit of rowan berries, a fruit so bitter that it is picked only after frost, with no single recorded origin.
french-whisky: France's whisky story begins in Brittany, where the Warenghem distillery at Lannion, a liqueur maker since the start of the twentieth century, began producing whisky in 1983 and is credited as the first in France to make and age it commercially. Its WB blend and later its Armorik single malt led the way for a French whisky scene that now draws on local barley, buckwheat and the country's plentiful wine casks.
swedish-whisky: Mackmyra, often called Sweden's first malt whisky distillery, was founded in 1999 by eight friends from Stockholm's Royal Institute of Technology, a year after a ski trip on which they wondered why Sweden made no whisky of its own. After years of trials they settled on their recipes, and their first limited release, Preludium 01, came out in February 2006 and sold out in under twenty minutes. Some Swedish malts are smoked with juniper as well as peat.
danish-whisky: One of the founding stories of Danish whisky began in May 2005, when nine friends in western Jutland set out to make whisky and called their project Stauning. They started in a building one of them owned, a former private slaughterhouse, floor-malting local barley and smoking some of it with peat from the Klosterlund Museum. Production moved to a farm and restarted there in 2009, and Stauning has stayed with local barley and floor malting ever since.
dutch-whisky: The Netherlands distilled grain as jenever for centuries before it turned to whisky. Two producers are counted as its whisky pioneers: the Us Heit brewery in Bolsward, Friesland, which began distilling Frysk Hynder in the early 2000s and is often credited with the first Dutch single malt, and Zuidam Distillers of Baarle-Nassau, whose Millstone whisky is made from grain milled in traditional windmills.
german-whisky: Germany's single malt story usually begins in Franconia in 1983, when Robert Fleischmann, who had founded the Blaue Maus distillery three years earlier to make fruit brandy, made his first attempt at a single malt at Eggolsheim; he sold his first whisky only in 1996. Blaue Maus is often cited as Germany's oldest whisky distillery. Whisky-making has since spread across the country, much of it from existing fruit-brandy and beer businesses, using wheat and spelt alongside barley.
austrian-whisky: Austrian whisky as a distillery business is usually dated to the mid-1990s, when the Haider family of Roggenreith, in the Waldviertel of Lower Austria, founded what is regarded as the country's first whisky distillery. Rye is grown across the district, and alongside single malt the Haiders became known for rye and rye malt whiskies. The family later opened a whisky visitor centre beside the distillery.
swiss-whisky: Swiss law long barred distilling grain and potatoes, which were reserved for food. The ban was lifted on 1 July 1999, and that day the Bader family's Holle distillery, on their farm at Lauwil, in Basel-Country, began making what is counted as the first Swiss single malt. Brewers such as Locher in Appenzell followed, and Swiss whisky often finishes in casks from the country's wine regions.
czech-whisky: The Czech single malt Hammerhead was distilled in 1989 at Prádlo, in the Plzeň region, where the distillery had spent several years working out a Scotch-style whisky from Czech barley. The Velvet Revolution swept away the regime that same year, and the casks were left to age largely forgotten. Stock Spirits, which later ran the distillery, found them in the late 2000s and bottled them as a single malt about two decades old.
finnish-whisky: For most of the twentieth century Finland's state alcohol monopoly kept distilling in few hands, and independent whisky arrived only after the rules eased. Teerenpeli, a brewery in Lahti, began distilling malt whisky in 2002, and Kyrö Distillery, set up in a former dairy at Isokyrö, followed with rye whisky, built on the idea that a country so fond of rye bread should have a rye whisky of its own.
icelandic-whisky: Icelandic whisky is closely tied to Eimverk, a distillery founded in 2009 that makes its spirits from Icelandic barley. Its Flóki whisky is named after Hrafna-Flóki, the Norse seafarer credited in the sagas with naming Iceland. One version is smoked with dried sheep dung rather than peat, a traditional Icelandic way of smoking food in a country with little wood to burn.
south-african-whisky: South Africa's modern whisky era dates from 1977, when Three Ships was launched as a blend of South African and Scotch whisky. It was first made by Stellenbosch Farmers Winery and since the early 1990s has been made at the James Sedgwick Distillery in Wellington, named after a nineteenth-century sea captain and liquor trader, on a distilling site that goes back to 1886. Sedgwick now makes both Three Ships and Bain's Cape Mountain whisky.
mexican-whisky: Mexican whisky took a distinctly native turn in the mid-2010s, when Douglas French, master distiller of Scorpion Mezcal in Oaxaca, brought out Sierra Norte, whiskies distilled mostly from native Oaxacan corn with a smaller share of barley and aged in French oak. Each bottling is named for the colour of its corn, among them yellow, white and black. Corn has been grown in Oaxaca for thousands of years, and the region's many native varieties give the whiskies their character.
chinese-whisky: Malt whisky in China took a major step in 2021, when Pernod Ricard began production at The Chuan, in the Emeishan area of Sichuan, billed as the first malt whisky distillery in China built by a major international drinks group. Diageo followed with a malt distillery in Eryuan County, Yunnan. Both investments are aimed at the largest spirits market in the world, and some Chinese whisky is matured at altitude in the south-west.
peated-single-malt: Peated single malt keeps the smoke of malt dried over burning peat, once the everyday fuel of Scottish maltings, so the style has no single origin beyond that old practice.
sherry-cask-single-malt: For generations Britain imported most of its sherry in cask, and Scotch distillers filled the emptied transport butts with whisky, which is how sherry's dried-fruit richness entered single malt. That supply dried up late in the twentieth century, as Spanish rules came to require sherry to be bottled at source. Distillers now commission Spanish bodegas to build new casks and season them with sherry purely to make whisky casks.
japanese-blended-whisky: Japanese whisky began with blends. Shinjiro Torii began building the Yamazaki distillery near Kyoto in 1923, with Masataka Taketsuru, who had studied distilling in Scotland, as its manager, and in 1929 they released Shirofuda, the first genuine Japanese whisky. Kakubin followed in 1937 and became a national standard. Because Japanese distillers have not traditionally traded stock with one another, each company has had to make the malt and grain components of its own blends.
mizunara-whisky: Japanese distillers turned to mizunara, their native oak, out of necessity: around the Second World War imported casks became almost impossible to obtain just as demand for whisky rose, so they had casks made from local wood. Mizunara proved porous, knotty and prone to leaks, and most distillers went back to American oak and sherry butts once they could. Only long maturation revealed its sandalwood, coconut and incense notes, and it is now one of the most coveted cask woods.
rye-malt-whiskey: Whiskey from 100% malted rye was revived in San Francisco by Fritz Maytag of Anchor Brewing, who opened a small distillery at the brewery in 1993 and set out to recreate an early American style of rye distilled in a pot still, at a time when rye whiskey had almost vanished. The result, Old Potrero, named after Potrero Hill, where the brewery stands, is often credited with helping to start American craft distilling.
american-light-whiskey: Light whisky was created by American regulators in 1968, as bourbon and rye lost ground to imported whiskies, gin and vodka. The new standard covered spirit distilled at more than 160 proof and aged in used or uncharred new oak, for whisky distilled from 26 January 1968, and labels could use the term from 1 July 1972. By the time the first light whiskies reached shelves, drinkers' tastes had moved on, and the category survives mainly as a curiosity.
grain-whisky: Grain whisky was made possible by the continuous still: Robert Stein developed one in Scotland in the late 1820s, and the Irishman Aeneas Coffey patented his improved column still in 1830. Distilling wheat or maize continuously gave a lighter, cheaper spirit that blenders married with pot-still malt, creating blended Scotch. Malt distillers argued it was not whisky at all until a Royal Commission ruled in 1909 that it was, and single grain bottlings now show it on its own.
triple-distilled-malt: Triple distillation is a long tradition of Irish whiskey and of Scotland's Lowlands, where Auchentoshan still runs every drop through three stills for a lighter, stronger new spirit.
navy-rum: The Royal Navy's rum ration began in 1655, after Britain took Jamaica and rum replaced beer aboard ship, and it was standardised by 1731. In 1740 Admiral Edward Vernon, nicknamed Old Grog for his grogram cloak, ordered it diluted with water, and the mixture became grog. Navy rum was a dark blend of Caribbean rums whose high bottling strength is still called Navy strength, linked by tradition to a gunpowder test of proof. The ration ended on 31 July 1970, remembered as Black Tot Day.
solera-rum: Solera rum borrows sherry's fractional blending, topping older casks with younger rum, and is made across Latin America, where the number on a label often names the oldest rum in the system.
rhum-vieux-agricole: Rhum agricole, distilled from fresh cane juice rather than molasses, rose in Martinique in the late nineteenth century, when European beet sugar collapsed cane sugar prices and planters turned their juice straight into rum. Homère Clément, a doctor and politician who bought the Domaine de l'Acajou in 1887, is often called the father of rhum agricole. Martinique gained a rum AOC in 1996, and its rules require rhum vieux to spend at least three years in oak, keeping the cane's grassy signature beneath the wood.
rhum-blanc-agricole: White rhum agricole is fresh cane-juice rum bottled unaged, from a style that took hold in the French Antilles in the late nineteenth century, when a slump in cane sugar prices sent planters distilling juice instead of molasses. In Martinique it falls under the island's rum AOC, whose rules govern cane varieties, harvest, fermentation and the column stills used. Rested briefly in steel and usually bottled at 50% or more, it is the most direct taste of fresh cane.
rhum-eleve-sous-bois: Élevé sous bois, raised under wood, is the middle grade of rhum agricole set out in the Martinique AOC: rum aged at least twelve months in oak but short of the three years required for vieux. Its straw-gold colour gives it a second name, rhum paille, straw rum. It belongs to the French islands' turn to distilling fresh cane juice in the late nineteenth century, and it is an everyday sipping rhum in Martinique and Guadeloupe.
cachaca-de-alambique: Cachaça de alambique is Brazil's pot-distilled artisanal cachaça, made in small batches on farms, above all in Minas Gerais, and distinct from the industrial column-distilled kind.
ron-anejo: Ron añejo is the aged rum style of the Spanish-speaking Caribbean, column-distilled and matured for several years in oak to a light, smooth finish, with no single recorded origin.
jamaican-wedderburn: Jamaica's distillers sort their rums into marks by ester content, the fruity compounds built by long fermentations, and Wedderburn names the heavy end of the classic scale, above Plummer and below Continental Flavoured. By the 1920s Plummer and Wedderburn rums were associated with Westmoreland and its rich flavours, and research into the names points to two London West India merchants, Thomas Plummer and John Wedderburn, rather than to Jamaican estates.
jamaican-plummer: Plummer is one of the historic Jamaican rum marks, the grades into which the island's distillers sort rum by ester content; on the classic scale it sits between the light Common Cleans and the heavy Wedderburns, at about 150 to 200 milligrams of esters per 100 millilitres of absolute alcohol. Research into the names points to British West India merchants, among them the London rum merchant Thomas Plummer, rather than to estates. By the 1920s Plummer rums were linked to Westmoreland.
blackstrap-rum: Blackstrap rum is made from the darkest, most exhausted grade of molasses, a heavy, mineral style from the Caribbean and the United States with no single recorded origin.
panamanian-rum: Panama's modern rum owes much to Francisco Fernández, known as Don Pancho, a Cuban rum master who spent decades in his country's rum industry before settling in Panama in the 1990s. There he revived and modernised the Las Cabras distillery, in Herrera province, and his Cuban methods shaped the light, column-still, tropically aged style for which Panama is now known.
venezuelan-rum: Rum has been made in Venezuela since colonial times, but its defining moment came in 2003, when the country granted Ron de Venezuela a controlled denomination of origin. Under its rules every rum, white included, must be made from Venezuelan cane and age at least two years in oak, a stricter minimum than most rum countries set. At the time only Chuao cocoa and Pecaya cocuy held such protection in Venezuela.
nicaraguan-rum: Nicaragua Sugar Estates was founded in 1890 at Chichigalpa, at the foot of the San Cristóbal volcano, with Francisco Alfredo Pellas, an Italian immigrant, as its main shareholder. Rum was made there from early on, but the Flor de Caña brand itself was registered in 1937, with Etiqueta Amarilla and Etiqueta Roja as its first bottlings. The Pellas family has run the business for five generations, and the volcano still appears on the label.
dominican-rum: The Dominican Republic's major rum houses date from the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries: Bermúdez traces itself to 1852, Brugal was founded at Puerto Plata in 1888 by Andrés Brugal Montaner, a Spanish-born merchant who had lived in Cuba, and Julián Barceló, a Spanish immigrant, founded Barceló in Santo Domingo around 1930. Dominican rules on what may be sold as Ron Dominicano require local cane and at least a year of ageing.
canazo: Cañazo is the artisanal cane spirit of Peru's warm Andean valleys, a long-standing rural drink with no single recorded origin, now being bottled with new care.
marie-galante-rhum: Marie-Galante, a small round island off Guadeloupe, keeps three working rum distilleries, Bielle, Bellevue and Poisson, the maker of Père Labat, all making rhum agricole from fresh cane juice. Sugar cane has shaped the island since the plantation era, and the ruins of the windmills that once crushed it still dot the fields. Its rhums are known for being bottled at 59%, a local custom.
mezcal-espadin: Espadín, Agave angustifolia, is the farmed agave behind the large majority of mezcal, cultivated across Oaxaca and ready to harvest in under a decade.
mezcal-tepeztate: Tepeztate is a wild Oaxacan agave that grows from cliff faces and can take around twenty-five years to mature, giving one of mezcal's most herbaceous expressions.
mezcal-madrecuixe: Madrecuixe is a wild Oaxacan agave of the karwinskii group, with a long narrow trunk instead of a round heart, giving a mineral, almost saline mezcal.
mezcal-arroqueno: Arroqueño is a huge, slow-growing Oaxacan agave, often wild-harvested and taking fifteen to twenty-five years to mature, giving a sweet, earthy and full-bodied mezcal.
mezcal-cuishe: Cuishe is a long-trunked karwinskii agave harvested mostly from the wild in Oaxaca, giving a dry, herbal mezcal with no recorded history of its own.
mezcal-ensamble: A mezcal ensamble is made by roasting and fermenting several agave varieties together, a producer's composition rather than a blend of finished spirits.
destilado-de-agave: Destilado de agave is the name for agave spirits made outside the mezcal denomination of origin, whether from an unlisted region or by an unapproved method, often by long-established makers.
flavoured-pink-gin: Pink gin once meant a Royal Navy drink of gin tinted with Angostura bitters, but the sweet, fruit-flavoured kind is a phenomenon of the late 2010s. Diageo launched Gordon's Premium Pink, flavoured with raspberry, strawberry and redcurrant, in 2017, and it helped set off a wave of pink gins across Britain. Because of their added sugar, many are legally classed as gin-based spirit drinks rather than gin.
old-tom-style-cream-gin: Cream gin is a clear gin redistilled with dairy cream, leaving a silky texture and faint sweetness behind, a rare style whose history is poorly documented.
gin-de-mahon: Gin reached Menorca during the British occupation of the eighteenth century, when the island began making a juniper spirit from wine alcohol for British sailors and soldiers. The style outlived the British, and the Pons family's Xoriguer distillery on Mahón harbour, named after an old family windmill, became its standard-bearer. Protected first as Gin de Menorca and later as Gin de Mahón, it is one of very few gins with its own geographical indication.
jonge-jenever: Jonge, young, jenever is a twentieth-century style. Around 1900 distillers became able to make an almost neutral spirit, and a growing taste for lighter drinks, together with shortages of imported grain and therefore of malt during the First World War, encouraged blends with less malt wine, much as blended whisky developed in Scotland. Today the rules cap jonge jenever at 15% malt wine. Young and old describe the recipe rather than age, so a jonge jenever can be cask-aged.
oude-jenever: Oude, old, jenever is the traditional malty style and older than gin itself. A Dutch ordinance of 1606 already taxed juniper spirits, and jenever appears in a play by Philip Massinger in 1623, which undermines the popular story that the physician Franciscus Sylvius, then a child, invented it. English soldiers who fought in the Low Countries took the taste home, a story often linked to the phrase Dutch courage. Today oude jenever must contain at least 15% malt wine.
mediterranean-gin: The Mediterranean style is best represented by Gin Mare, created around 2010 by the Giró family, long in the drinks business, in a converted chapel in the fishing town of Vilanova i la Geltrú, on the coast south-west of Barcelona. Its key botanicals come from around the sea: Arbequina olives from Spain, rosemary from Greece, thyme from Turkey and basil from Italy. It rode the Spanish passion for gin and tonic served in large balloon glasses over plenty of ice.
german-gin: Germany's gin boom is closely tied to Monkey 47, launched in 2010 by Alexander Stein, a former Nokia manager, with 47 botanicals at 47% in the northern Black Forest. Its makers tell of a recipe left by Montgomery Collins, an RAF wing commander who settled in the Black Forest after the war and ran a guesthouse called Zum wilden Affen, and of a box found decades later holding his gin, a letter and a list of ingredients. Many German gins have since followed.
french-gin: Citadelle's makers trace their inspiration to the late eighteenth century, when a royal privilege allowed two distillers, Carpeau and Stival, to make genièvre at the citadel of Dunkirk for gin-loving England. Alexandre Gabriel of Cognac Ferrand won permission to use his Cognac pot stills for gin outside the brandy season and in 1996 unveiled Citadelle, named after that citadel. It opened the way for a French gin scene that often uses grape spirit and borrows from perfumery and wine.
nordic-gin: Nordic gin is a modern style built on foraged Scandinavian botanicals such as dill, caraway, lingonberry and birch, drawing on the north's long habit of flavouring with wild juniper.
mexican-gin: Mexican gin is a young category distilled with native botanicals such as cempasúchil marigold, avocado leaf and damiana, often on an agave or cane spirit base.
bathtub-gin: Bathtub gin is compound gin: botanicals or flavourings steeped in finished spirit rather than redistilled with it. It became notorious during American Prohibition, when illicit makers mixed industrial or bootleg alcohol with juniper oil and glycerine in large containers. The name is usually explained by the bathtubs used for mixing, or by bottles too tall to top up from a sink tap, and neither story can be proved. Modern bathtub gins revive the compound method legitimately.
damson-gin: Damson gin is an English hedgerow liqueur of damsons steeped in gin with sugar, made at home each autumn in the manner of sloe gin, and its origins are not recorded.
rye-vodka: The Polish word wódka first appears in court records from Sandomierz in 1405, for alcohol-based medicines and cosmetics, and by the sixteenth century the drinking spirit was called gorzałka. In 1693 Jakub Kazimierz Haur published detailed recipes for making vodka from rye, the grain that suited Poland's poorer soils. Rye remains the classic Polish style, and spirit sold as Polish vodka must now be distilled in Poland from traditional Polish grains or potatoes.
wheat-vodka: Wheat vodka is the lightest and softest of the grain styles, made in Russia, Poland and France and used by many premium Western brands, with no single recorded origin.
grape-vodka: Grape vodka moved into the mainstream with Cîroc, launched in 2003. Developed for Diageo by Jean-Sébastien Robicquet, it is distilled from grapes rather than grain, chiefly Mauzac Blanc from Gaillac and Ugni Blanc, with the final distillation at the Distillerie de Chevanceaux. The name combines the French cime, summit, and roche, rock, a nod to the high vineyards some of the grapes come from.
whey-vodka: Whey vodka is distilled from the lactose in leftover cheesemaking whey, a dairy by-product turned into spirit in New Zealand and Ireland, with no single recorded origin.
khrenovukha: Khrenovukha is a Russian household infusion of vodka with horseradish, honey and sometimes lemon, and the stories tying it to Peter the Great remain unsourced.
